quote: Well, I saw this thing about the Tesla panels. And they said, if you can fit this in your yard, and I looked and it was just a small panel.
stewart_read: This is the customer-expectation-gap the schema anticipates: he expected Tesla-branded panels, not Ion's product. The rep does address it directly at 01:19, which is the correct move per schema guidance to only reframe when the customer raises it.
coaching_implication: Confirm rep continues reframing only when the gap surfaces (as done here) rather than over-explaining preemptively — this instance was handled correctly and can be used as a positive example.

quote: I'm taking a look, and it looks like you have too much shade for us to make our system work anyway. So I'll just get back to us for now.
stewart_read: The rep issues a same-call DQ based on a satellite/imaging read very quickly, without asking the customer any verify questions about the roof or exploring the ground-mount idea the customer volunteers seconds later. It's genuinely unclear whether this is a failure or a recognized fast-screening workflow — the schema itself references satellite imaging as an existing Ion tool, so real-time shade screening may be standard practice here, not a shortcut the rep invented.
alternative_hypothesis: Strategic: if satellite-assisted shade screening is a legitimate, sanctioned Ion tool for fast DQ, then closing quickly here is efficient and correct, and the coaching gap is not the DQ itself but the lack of follow-up on the customer's workaround idea raised immediately after.
coaching_implication: Manager should confirm with Kenny whether satellite-based instant DQ is standard procedure. If yes, the coaching point narrows to: after DQing, still acknowledge and briefly explore the customer's own proposed workaround before closing it off, since he volunteers it unprompted.

quote: if they build racks in the back part of my yard, that would solve the problem. But, they didn't wanna hear that.
stewart_read: Ion has no ground-mount/rack offering per the schema (roof-mounted systems only), so there is no cross-sell or exception path to route this to — this is not a missed cross-sell, it's a closure-quality gap: the customer flags he's been dismissed on this idea before, and the rep's response doesn't acknowledge that frustration or explain why racks aren't an option beyond restating policy.
alternative_hypothesis: There may genuinely be nothing to route here since Ion doesn't offer ground-mount systems — the miss isn't a lost sale, it's an unaddressed repeat-frustration signal from the customer.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to name the pattern back to the customer ("sounds like you've run into that same answer before") rather than just repeating the policy — costs nothing and prevents the customer feeling stonewalled twice in one call.

quote: Unfortunately, my company, we also only do roof mounted systems, so I apologize about that as well.
stewart_read: Rep does apologize and is polite, which is a partial rapport gesture, but it's the second flat restatement of the same limitation without engaging the customer's underlying idea.
coaching_implication: The apology is fine but insufficient on its own after a repeated dismissal signal — pair politeness with a specific acknowledgment of what the customer said.

quote: Yeah. I just wish a little bit. Yeah.
stewart_read: The customer voices genuine disappointment in Tesla's mission ('they've gone astray') as a distinct emotional beat from the DQ itself — closer to venting than a sales objection — and the rep does not acknowledge it at all, moving straight into answering the technical question that follows.
alternative_hypothesis: Reactive: the rep may simply not have registered this as anything beyond small talk given the call was already effectively over post-DQ.
coaching_implication: Not a high-stakes miss since the lead is DQ'd, but worth flagging as a pattern: rep answers the literal question asked and skips the emotional content underneath it, even when there's no sales pressure driving that omission.

quote: That that the the Tesla panels, they that's something only Tesla does. We're a certified Tesla arm installer, but only for their batteries.
stewart_read: Rep's framing is imprecise against the schema's clarified relationship (Ion sells its own panels + Tesla Powerwall battery + in-house roofing; the schema does not describe Ion as a 'Tesla arm installer' for batteries only) — this could confuse a customer further rather than clarify.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may be using shorthand that is functionally accurate at the point-of-call even if it doesn't match the schema's precise wording.
coaching_implication: Have the rep use the clean framing: 'Tesla referred your inquiry to us — we install our own panels plus Tesla's Powerwall battery' rather than 'certified Tesla arm installer... only for their batteries,' which undersells Ion's own panel product.

quote: Not usually. I mean, it's it's their their main thing is the shingles right now. That's what they're pushing for is the shingles.
stewart_read: After the lead is already DQ'd, the rep spends real time giving a detailed technical explanation of a competitor's (Tesla's) product line — this is closer-tier or even out-of-scope content with zero pipeline value since there's no appointment to protect.
alternative_hypothesis: Strategic: rep may be extending simple customer service/goodwill on a dead lead rather than trying to sell anything, which costs little since the call is already closed.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to redirect general product-education questions to a quick close ('That's a great question for our team, but I want to respect your time') rather than open-ended technical explanation, even post-DQ — habit reinforcement matters regardless of whether this specific call had anything left to lose.
